verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, with stringed-music, upon the Eighth; a psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the one who leads the music: to be sung with strings, upon the eighth. A psalm, David's.
verses.directors_commentary:
A superscription is a stage direction, and this one is dense. The first word names the temple's chief musician, the one who 'oversees' the performance, a reminder that this private groan was handed to the community as a liturgy. The text says to be sung with 'stringed music' and 'upon the Eighth' (Hebrew sheminit). Nobody knows exactly what that means. The medieval commentators in the packet divide: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and the Targum take it as an instrument of eight strings; Ibn Ezra also allows an eighth melody or mode; Radak reports the Talmudic suggestion that it concerns the eighth day, which he calls remote. Modern scholars add the octave, a low pitch, or an eight-stringed lyre. Tell the actors to hear a low, dark sound rather than a precise mode.

The KJV gives 'To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith' and counts all this as 'verse 0', so every verse in the English Bible is numbered one behind the Hebrew. The attribution 'of David' (ledavid) may mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of' David; the later tradition (Malbim) places it after the Bathsheba affair, which is an inference not stated here.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'the eighth'. It names an instrument, a tuning, or a mode; the same word appears with a different musical term in 1 Chr 15:21. Rashi takes it as an eight-stringed lyre.
'To the one who oversees / leads'. The verb נצח means 'to be pre-eminent, to supervise'; in the psalm titles it names the musical director.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, not in your anger may you rebuke me, and not in your wrath may you discipline me.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD — not in your anger. Do not rebuke me while your anger burns; do not correct me in the heat of your wrath.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with the divine name and a flat negative. The speaker does not deny the rebuke; he asks that it not come in anger. He assumes the sickness is a verdict, which was normal in the ancient world: illness was understood as divine disfavour, not an accident of germs. Radak hears this as a plea for measure, citing Jeremiah's 'correct me, LORD, but with justice' (Jer 10:24); Meiri reads it as the sufferer admitting his sins brought this, but asking for the pace he can bear.

The Hebrew sets two pairs in parallel: 'anger' (ʾaf, literally 'nose', the flared nostril) and 'wrath' (ḥemah, heat), and 'rebuke' (yakhaḥ) and 'discipline' (yasar). Malbim finds a difference: anger is visible, wrath burns hidden; rebuke is speech, discipline is blows. The KJV's 'rebuke … chasten … hot displeasure' is fair, but 'displeasure' drains the heat out of ḥemah, and 'chasten' sounds like a church rite rather than a father's hand. BBE's 'be bitter with me' mistranslates.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'in your nose': the nostril that flares or snorts, an image of anger. English loses the body in 'anger'.
'discipline, correct'. It is the word for a father's training of a child, which makes the request a plea to be treated as a son, not an enemy; Malbim draws the same point.

verses.translation_literal: Be gracious to me, YHWH, for I [am] withered; heal me, YHWH, for my bones are terrified.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, LORD, for I am wasted, cut down to nothing. Heal me, LORD — my very bones are shaking.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two petitions, each with its reason, each opened by the name. The first reason is 'I am withered' (ʾumlal). The word is a rare, passive-sounding adjective for a plant that has dried or a person cut off from strength; Rashi glosses it 'spoiled and weak of strength', Radak and Meiri tie it to 'cutting off', Metzudat Zion to the root of 'circumcision' as cutting. It is not simply 'weak' as in KJV; it is a body that has been cut down.

The second reason is 'my bones are terrified'. The verb bahal means to be panicked or dismayed; it is a word for an emotion, and applying it to bones is the point. The bones are the frame of the body, so Radak and Meiri read 'bones' as the whole body. The KJV's 'vexed' sounds like annoyance; the Hebrew is shudder and dread. The verb comes back in verses 4 and 11 and ties the psalm together.

philological_notes.note: 'Withered, languishing'; related to the cutting off and drying of a plant. Rashi and Radak cite Neh 3:34 and 1 Sam 2:5 as parallels.
'Terrified, thrown into panic'. The same root recurs in 6:4 (of the soul) and 6:11 (of the enemies), tying the three together.

verses.translation_literal: And my soul is terrified exceedingly, and you, YHWH — until when?
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul is shaking too, shaken to its depths. And you, LORD — how long?
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse breaks off mid-sentence. 'And you, YHWH — until when?' has no verb, and the silence is the line. The commentators each fill it differently. Rashi supplies 'will you look on and not heal?'; Radak and Meiri supply 'until when will you strike me and not heal me?' (Meiri: until when will you prolong my illness and crush me with these afflictions). Ibn Ezra completes it the other way, turned back on the speaker: 'until when will my soul be terrified, having no strength to bear it?'. Do not supply anything: let the actor stop.

The sufferer moves from body to self. 'Bones' were the frame; 'soul' (nefesh) is the whole living person, with the throat that breathes and craves. The same verb bahal ties them: the bones are terrified, and then the soul, 'exceedingly' (me'od). Ibn Ezra says the soul, bound to the body, is more terrified than the body, which is why the word 'exceedingly' is here; Radak says it fears dying of this illness. KJV 'sore vexed' again reads as irritation; the Hebrew is shudder and dread. The question 'how long?' is the usual lament cry of the psalms; it aims the accusation at God, not at the illness. A note on the text: the written form 've'attah' is spelled without the final he ('ve'at', Ketiv) and read with it (Qere); Radak says they are one word and compares Num 11:15.

philological_notes.note: 'My self, my life, my throat'. Not an immortal soul in the later sense: it is the living being, which is why it can be rescued from death in v. 5.
'Until when?' A fixed lament formula; here it is left without a verb, and the medieval commentators each complete it differently.

verses.translation_literal: Return, YHWH! Rescue my soul! Save me, for the sake of your steadfast love.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn back to me, LORD. Pull my life out of this. Save me — for your faithful love's sake.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three imperatives in a row, short as gasps. 'Return' (shuvah) assumes that God has gone away, or turned away in anger; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'return from your wrath'. It is also the psalm's turn, since shuv recurs in v. 11 for the enemies who turn back. 'Rescue' (ḥalletzah) is literally 'draw out, pull free', as one is pulled from a pit or a snare (Metzudat Zion, who compares Hos 5:6); Rashi and Radak take it as rescue from the illness, so that the speaker does not die of it.

The ground of the request is ḥesed, covenant loyalty, the faithfulness God has bound himself to, and not the speaker's own record. Radak puts it plainly: 'not by my righteousness, for I know that I am guilty'; Meiri calls the whole line a confession. The KJV's 'mercies' (plural) is the least accurate of the English versions: the Hebrew is one word, singular, and it is a bond, not a feeling of pity. 'Lovingkindness' (ASV) is nearer. Nothing in the verse about forgiveness; the speaker asks only to live.

philological_notes.note: 'Your covenant loyalty, steadfast love'. A word of obligation freely taken on, not mere kindness.
'Draw out, pull free, rescue'. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'draw out' and compares Hos 5:6.

verses.translation_literal: For [there is] no remembrance of you in death; in Sheol, who gives thanks to you?
verses.translation_dramatic: For in death no one speaks your name. In Sheol, who is left to thank you?
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalmist makes his case to God as a matter of self-interest: a dead worshipper is no worshipper. This is not an argument against an afterlife as later centuries understood it; it states what ancient Israel generally assumed, that Sheol, the underworld of the dead, was a place of silence, cut off from the praise and temple that sustained the bond with YHWH. Hezekiah makes the same argument in Isaiah 38:18, which Radak cites, and Ps 115:17 repeats it.

The 'remembrance' (zekher) is liturgical: to recall the name in worship and in the thanksgiving offering. The verb here, yodeh, means to confess, acknowledge, give thanks in public. The medieval commentators soften the claim: Radak and Meiri say it is the body that lies dumb, while the soul praises, or that the point is the loss of the chance to do good while alive. The KJV renders Sheol as 'the grave', which narrows a realm of the dead to a hole in the ground.

philological_notes.note: 'In Sheol', the realm of the dead; not a place of punishment, but of silence and weakness. The KJV 'grave' is a loose translation.
'Confesses, gives public thanks'. The same verb serves for praise and for confession; the sense is a public acknowledgment.

verses.translation_literal: I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed swim; with my tear[s] I melt my couch.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am worn out with groaning. Every night I float my bed in weeping; I dissolve the couch beneath me with tears.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most physical verse of the psalm, and it is deliberately overdone. Radak says outright that 'swim' and 'melt' are hyperbole (hafla'ah), and Meiri agrees. Two verbs, two pieces of furniture: 'bed' (mittah) and 'couch' (ʿeres, a framed bed such as a rich man might have), parallel as in Hebrew verse. The first verb, asheh, is the verb for swimming (Isa 25:11, cited by Rashi and Metzudat Zion); the second, amseh, is 'to dissolve' (the same verb used of hearts that 'melt' in fear, as Radak notes at Josh 14:8). The man is not just crying; his bed is afloat.

The Hebrew has a plain 'tear' in the singular (collective), where the KJV says 'tears'. The KJV 'I water my couch' is tame; 'make my bed to swim' is nearer. YLT 'I meditate' is a lexical error, Rashi's 'soil with filth' is possible but unlikely. Night is the setting because the sickbed is worst in the dark when no one sees (Radak).

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of שׂחה 'to swim': 'I make [the bed] swim'. Rashi alternatively links it to 'filth'; Ibn Ezra reports an Aramaic 'wash'.
'I dissolve, I soak until it melts'; the verb used of melting hearts.
'My couch, my bedstead'; a framed bed, a higher word than 'mittah'.

verses.translation_literal: My eye has wasted away from vexation; it has grown old because of all my adversaries.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eye is eaten away with vexation; it has grown old, grown dim, with all that those who press on me have done.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tears have worn out the sight. 'Wasted' (ʿashshah) is related to the word for a moth: the eye is moth-eaten (Ibn Ezra and Radak cite Isa 50:9; Metzudat Zion cites Ps 31:11, 'my bones wasted away'; Meiri the same). Rashi adds a second sense, a dim eye, as if seen through glass.

The second verb, ʿatqah, is disputed. Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David take it as 'grown old': the eye has aged and dimmed, as in old age. Radak prefers a different root sense, 'moved from its place', as in 'the rock is moved from its place' (Job 14:18), and notes that others, among them the Targum and Rashi, say 'grown old'; Meiri reports both readings. Radak says both verbs are exaggeration, as in v. 7. The English versions all follow 'grown old'.

The cause is kaʿas, which is vexation or provocation, anger and resentment as much as sorrow; the KJV's 'grief' is milder than the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the sufferer's anger at the gloating of those who watch his sickness. The source is 'all my adversaries' (tzorerai), literally 'those who bind me in a tight place'. Their presence at his bedside is what makes the illness worse: the enemy visits to see him fail. This turns the lament from sickness to social hostility.

philological_notes.note: 'Has wasted, rotted, been moth-eaten'; related to עָשׁ 'moth' (Isa 50:9) and used of the bones in Ps 31:11 (Hebrew numbering).
Either 'has grown old' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David) or 'has moved from its place' (Radak, citing Job 14:18); Meiri gives both. The literal layer follows the first.
'Those who bind / press / are hostile to me'; a participle, not a noun for 'enemy' as such.

verses.translation_literal: Turn away from me, all [you] workers of iniquity, for YHWH has heard the sound of my weeping.
verses.translation_dramatic: Away from me, all of you who work wickedness! The LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns in the middle of a line, with no transition. The tone changes from complaint to command: 'Turn away from me', addressed to the people who stood over the sickbed in v. 8. Nothing in the text explains why; the reason given is simply 'for YHWH has heard'. The verb is in the perfect, 'has heard', so the speaker acts as though the answer has already come. Many readers think a priest or prophet delivered an oracle between the lines (a reconstruction, not in the text).

The phrase 'workers of iniquity' (poʿale ʾaven) is common in the psalms for people who do harm; ʾaven carries the sense of trouble and emptiness. The 'sound of my weeping' is the key phrase: the tears that dissolved the couch in v. 7 are what God heard, so the weeping itself is the prayer. The KJV 'Depart' is archaic but accurate; 'the voice of my weeping' is literal. The same phrase turns up in a promise made to Hezekiah: 'I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears' (Isa 38:5).

philological_notes.note: 'Doers of trouble / wickedness'. The expression is stock in the psalms for those who plot harm.
'The sound of my weeping'; the phrase makes the weeping itself a form of address to God.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has heard my plea for grace; YHWH will take my prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has heard my cry for mercy. The LORD will take up my prayer.
verses.directors_commentary:
A verse of two halves, nearly the same, built as a chiasm: the first opens with the verb ('has heard'), then the name, then the plea; the second opens with the name, then the prayer, and ends on the verb ('will take'). The name stands at the centre, doubled, and the verbs hold the two ends. Metzudat David calls it a doubling for emphasis, which is the usual Hebrew device. But the verbs differ. 'Has heard' is perfect: it is finished. 'Will take' (yiqqaḥ) is imperfect, and Radak reads it as present and future both ('now and whenever my prayer comes to him'), or as equivalent to the past; Ibn Ezra and Meiri gloss it 'receive'.

The nouns also differ: techinnah, a plea for grace (from the same root as 'be gracious' in v. 3), and tefillah, the general word for prayer. The speaker has asked for 'grace' in v. 3 and now says he has been heard. The verb 'take' (laqaḥ) is the one used for accepting an offering or a gift: God receives the prayer as he would an offering. Ibn Ezra adds 'or he will take it in place of a burnt offering'. The KJV 'receive' is fine here; BBE's 'let come before him' is a paraphrase.

philological_notes.note: 'My plea for favour'; from the root of 'be gracious' in v. 3, so the request of v. 3 comes back as the thing God has heard.
'Will take / accept'. Radak reads it as present-and-future, or as the past 'has taken'; the verb is the one for accepting a gift.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed and terrified exceedingly, all my enemies; may they turn back, may they be ashamed in a moment.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be shamed — let them be shaken to the bone, every one who is my enemy. Let them turn and flee, and be put to shame in an instant.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends by turning its own words around. The verb that described the speaker's bones (v. 3) and soul (v. 4), bahal, 'terrified', is now wished on the enemies. Ibn Ezra notices: 'terrified' here answers the earlier 'my bones are terrified, my soul is terrified'. The fear passes to those who gloated. The same happens with 'turn' (shuv): in v. 5 the speaker begged God to turn back; now the enemies are told to turn back. The sufferer who asked to be healed wants those watching him to be seen for what they are.

The last word is 'in a moment' (rega'), the opposite of the 'how long?' of v. 4: after the long night, the reversal comes in an instant.

The verbs can be read two ways. The forms are imperfects that may be jussive, a wish ('let them be ashamed', KJV, BBE, Webster), or plain imperfects, a prediction ('they shall be ashamed', ASV; YLT even makes it present). The dramatic layer chooses the wish, because it fits the pleading voice of the whole psalm, but the Hebrew does not force it.

'Turn back' is also open. Rashi has a famous midrash on the double 'ashamed': the wicked are shamed twice, once at judgment and once when God has them shown their own record again. Radak and Metzudat David take it as the enemies returning to be at peace with the speaker (Radak: when they see their plan has failed, they will return to me to be at peace); Ibn Ezra gives 'they will relent, or seek my peace'; Meiri has 'they turn back from their schemes'. KJV's 'let them return' keeps the ambiguity.

philological_notes.note: 'And may they be terrified'; the same root as 'my bones are terrified' (6:3) and 'my soul is terrified' (6:4), now turned on the enemies.
'A moment, an instant'; the shortest unit of time, set against 'until when?' of v. 4.

'May they turn back'; ambiguous between retreat in defeat and repentance. Radak and Metzudat David take it as turning to make peace; Ibn Ezra as relenting or seeking peace; Meiri as turning from their schemes; Rashi relates it to the second judgment in the midrash.
